blurb: How a raw text predictor becomes a helpful assistant: fine-tuning, human feedback, DPO and RL for reasoning.

cards.title: Three stages after pretraining

steps.p: The model trains on example conversations showing ideal assistant replies, learning the format and tone of a helpful answer.
It then learns from comparisons — which of two replies is better — to sharpen judgment beyond imitation.
Further rounds handle safety, tool use, coding and reasoning, often with reinforcement learning against automated checks.

cards.aside: Pretraining gives knowledge; post-training gives behavior.

cards.q: Supervised fine-tuning data for a chat model consists mainly of…
options: Prompts paired with high-quality responses to imitate
cards.why: Demonstrations. Each example is a prompt and an ideal reply, written by people or strong models. The model is trained to produce the reply given the prompt.

cards.statement: In OpenAI's InstructGPT study, people preferred outputs of a 1.3B tuned model over the original 175B GPT-3.
cards.why: True. The 2022 paper found raters preferred the 100× smaller model after instruction tuning and RLHF. Alignment to what users want mattered more than raw size.

cards.title: To the model, a chat is just one long sequence of tokens.
cards.detail: Special tokens mark where system, user and assistant turns begin and end. The "conversation" structure exists only because post-training taught the model to respect those markers.

cards.q: Ask a base model "What is the capital of France?" and it might reply with…
options: "What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Spain?"
cards.why: More of the same pattern. On the web, a question is often followed by more questions, such as in a quiz list. The base model continues the document instead of answering.

cards.statement: Post-training has historically used far less compute than pretraining.
cards.why: True. Traditionally a small fraction. That is changing as reinforcement learning for reasoning models scales up, with some labs reporting much larger RL budgets.

cards.title: Learning from human preferences

steps.p: The model writes several replies to each prompt, and people pick which they prefer.
A separate model learns to predict those preferences, outputting a score for any prompt and reply.
The assistant is then trained with reinforcement learning (often PPO) to earn high scores, while a penalty keeps it close to its starting behavior.

cards.aside: The reward model is a learned stand-in for human judgment — useful, but exploitable.

cards.q: A reward model in RLHF takes a prompt and a response and outputs…
options: A single score of how good the response is
cards.why: A scalar score. It is usually the language model itself with its output layer replaced by a single number, trained so preferred replies score higher.

cards.q: Reward models are commonly trained with the Bradley–Terry model, where the probability A beats B is…
cards.why: sigmoid(rA − rB). Only the difference in scores matters. The same model ranks chess players and sports teams.

cards.statement: Labelers usually compare two responses rather than scoring each one on an absolute scale, because comparisons are more consistent.
cards.why: True. People disagree about whether a reply deserves a 6 or a 7, but agree much more on which of two is better.

cards.title: RLHF-trained models tend to tell people what they want to hear.
cards.detail: Anthropic research (Sharma et al., 2023) found assistants often shift answers to match a user's stated opinion, partly because human raters reward agreement. This is called sycophancy.

cards.q: Reward models often favor longer answers regardless of quality. This is an example of…
options: Reward hacking — exploiting a flaw in the proxy reward
cards.why: Reward hacking. If length correlates with preference in the training data, the policy learns to pad. Labs counter it by penalizing length or improving the reward model.

cards.title: Preference tuning without RL

steps.p: Direct Preference Optimization (2023) showed the RLHF objective can be rewritten so no separate reward model or sampling loop is needed.
Given a chosen and a rejected reply, DPO raises the chosen reply's likelihood relative to a frozen reference model, and lowers the rejected one's.
It is just a supervised loss: simpler, cheaper and more stable than PPO, so many open models adopted it.

cards.aside: The paper's subtitle summed it up: "Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model."

cards.q: What does DPO need that RLHF with PPO also needs?
options: Pairs of preferred and rejected responses
cards.why: Preference pairs. Both start from human (or AI) comparisons. DPO skips the reward model, the sampling and the value network that PPO uses.

cards.statement: DPO still uses a frozen copy of the starting model as a reference.
cards.why: True. The loss compares the policy's probabilities to the reference's, which plays the role of RLHF's KL penalty and stops the model drifting too far.

cards.q: Anthropic's Constitutional AI replaces many human labels with…
options: AI feedback guided by a written set of principles
cards.why: AI feedback. A model critiques and compares responses using a list of principles (a "constitution"), producing preference data at scale. This approach is often called RLAIF.

cards.title: AI-generated preference labels can work about as well as human ones for some tasks.
cards.detail: A 2023 Google study found RLAIF matched RLHF on summarization and dialogue tasks, suggesting much preference data can be produced by models, with humans focusing on hard or high-stakes cases.

cards.statement: Offline methods like DPO and online RL methods behave identically.
cards.why: False. Online RL learns from the model's own fresh samples; DPO learns from a fixed dataset. Studies often find online methods better on hard tasks, at higher cost.

cards.title: Rewards you can check

steps.p: For math with known answers or code with unit tests, correctness can be checked automatically — no human judge needed.
The model attempts many problems, and RL reinforces whatever reasoning led to correct answers.
Models trained this way learn to write long chains of thought: trying approaches, checking work, backtracking.

cards.aside: This is the core recipe behind OpenAI's o-series and DeepSeek-R1.

cards.q: DeepSeek's GRPO algorithm avoids training a separate critic model by…
options: Comparing each answer to the average reward of a group of answers to the same prompt
cards.why: Group baselines. Sample several answers per prompt; each one's advantage is its reward relative to the group's mean. That removes PPO's value network and its memory cost.

cards.title: DeepSeek-R1-Zero learned to reason at length using reinforcement learning alone, with no example reasoning to copy.
cards.detail: Trained only with rewards for correct answers and format, it spontaneously began writing longer solutions and re-checking its work. The paper highlighted an "aha moment" where it paused to reconsider.

cards.statement: RL with verifiable rewards works best in domains where answers can be checked automatically.
cards.why: True. Math, code and formal puzzles are ideal. Open-ended writing has no simple checker, so it still relies on reward models or human preferences.

cards.q: DeepSeek fine-tuned small Qwen and Llama models on R1's reasoning traces. This technique is called…
cards.why: Distillation. A strong teacher generates outputs, and a smaller student learns to imitate them. The distilled models reasoned far better than their size suggested.

cards.title: Ask for the critique before the answer
cards.body: Reasoning improves when a model checks itself. Asking it to list what could be wrong with a draft, then revise, often beats asking for a perfect answer in one shot.
cards.challenge: Next time you use an AI for something important, add: "First list the weaknesses of your answer, then give a revised one."
